title: The voice in the desert (Matthew 3:1–12)
hook: John the Baptist in camel hair, eating locusts, calling people to turn around

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hidden years: thirty years in Nazareth, and almost nothing written down. Your line was most of his life was ordinary. What ordinary thing did you do carefully? Day thirty-one. Today the quiet ends, with a shout from the desert.

Out past the towns, in the dry country near the Jordan River, a man is shouting. He wears a rough garment of camel's hair with a leather belt. He eats locusts and wild honey. No house, no title, no invitation. And people come. Matthew says they came out from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan, out into the dry country to hear him. They stood in the river, confessed their sins, and he baptized them in the water. This is John, the one Christians call the Baptist. He's a relative of Jesus, and his message fits in one breath. Today: what he was shouting, and the road he wanted built.
screen: `A MAN SHOUTING IN THE DESERT.` → `CAMEL HAIR, LOCUSTS, WILD HONEY.` → `AND THE CROWDS COME.`

segments.voice: Here is John's message in the Douay-Rheims Bible, the old Catholic English translation: "Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." The King James says repent. Both are reaching for one Greek word, metanoia. Meta, after or beyond. Noia, from the word for mind. A change of mind. A turning around. Not a feeling bad, first of all. A new direction. The Douay-Rheims followed the Latin Bible, which says do penance, and that wording is one reason Catholics speak of the sacrament of penance: confession carries an echo of this call to turn. Then Matthew reaches back to the prophet Isaiah, centuries earlier, and hears John in it: "A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." Isaiah's picture is a road made ready for a king: the low places filled, the hills brought down, the crooked made straight. John says: a king is coming, and the road is you. And John is not gentle about it. When religious leaders come to watch, he tells them to bring forth fruit worthy of penance, to show the turning in how they live. The axe, he says, is already at the root of the trees. But he points away from himself. Someone mightier is coming after him, he says, and he isn't worthy even to carry his sandals. The Church keeps John close. His voice fills the Sundays of Advent, and his birth has its own feast, on June twenty-fourth, as well as his death.
screen: `DO PENANCE: THE KINGDOM IS AT HAND.` · `METANOIA — A CHANGE OF MIND.` · `A KING IS COMING. FIX THE ROAD.` · `HE POINTS AWAY FROM HIMSELF.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing to turn from. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Not your whole life. One thing. A habit that keeps making the road crooked. A sharp way you talk to someone. A scroll you can't stop. A grudge you keep feeding. Find it and name it, plainly, inside. You don't have to fix it now. Just turn and face it. If you pray, you can hold it up to God and ask for help turning. If you don't, just sit with the naming. The bell holds the time.
The voice in the desert. John the Baptist, calling people to turn around and make the road ready for someone greater. Today's word.
screen: `THE VOICE IN THE DESERT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: make straight the way. Today, straighten one small crooked thing: a message you owe, an apology, a promise you let slide. Fill one pothole. Day thirty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John the Baptist's call in the Advent Sunday readings and answer it in the sacrament of penance (confession), where a person names their sins, receives absolution and is given a penance.

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
pairs: a change of mind, a turning

myth: "do penance" and "repent" translate the same Greek word
both render metanoia, a change of mind. the Douay-Rheims follows the Latin, the King James the Greek.
John the Baptist and John the apostle are the same person
two different Johns. the Baptist prepared the way; the apostle was one of the twelve.
John says he is the one everyone is waiting for
he points away from himself: someone mightier is coming, whose sandals he isn't worthy to carry.

fork.setup: you're John. religious leaders come out to the river to see what you're doing. what do you say?
options: welcome them warmly and baptize them first.
tell them to show their turning by how they live.
send them away without a word.
fork.reveal: he challenges them: bring forth fruit worthy of penance. the turning has to show up in a life, not only at a riverbank.

original.note: Greek: a change of mind, a turning around. The Latin Bible rendered John's call as do penance.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wild man in the desert telling people they're bad.
what it means: a voice clearing the road, calling people to turn around because someone greater is coming.
what a scholar hears: metanoia, a change of mind. the Latin paenitentiam agite, do penance, gave the Douay-Rheims its wording and the sacrament its old name.

sources.quoted: Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths.

notes: Quotations of Matthew 3:2 and 3:3 are given from the Challoner Douay-Rheims from memory; confirm wording and punctuation.
The carry 'make straight the way' matches John 1:23 ('make straight the way of the Lord'); Matthew 3:3 in Douay-Rheims reads 'make straight his paths'. Both are used; confirm.
Metanoia etymology (meta + nous) and the Vulgate 'paenitentiam agite' as the source of 'do penance': confirm, and confirm the link to the name 'sacrament of penance' is fairly stated.
'Fruit worthy of penance' (3:8) and 'not worthy to bear his shoes' (3:11) are paraphrased, not quoted.
Feasts: Nativity of John the Baptist June 24 (solemnity), Passion/Beheading August 29. Stated as 'one of very few saints whose birth has its own feast' (with Mary and Jesus); confirm phrasing.
Softened: the script now says the Latin wording is 'one reason' for the name 'sacrament of penance', not its sole source.
Dating of Isaiah 40: many scholars date Isaiah 40–55 to the sixth century BC (the exile). The script says only 'centuries earlier'.
Editor review (2026-10-01): the road-crew picture is now Isaiah's own image (40:4) rather than unsourced history; cut 'one of very few saints' and 'walking for hours'.
